name: Unfair Commercial Practices Directive
evidence_rating: moderate: one causal study (DiD) on trust and cross-border shopping; two Commission fitness checks with cost and detriment estimates; prevalence studies show persistent online harm
summary: The UCPD replaced national rules on misleading and aggressive selling in 2005-2007. One causal study finds it raised consumer trust and cross-border shopping, but only in countries with weak protection beforehand. The Commission's 2017 and 2024 reviews found the rules cheap to comply with (about EUR 0.5-0.7 billion a year for the three core consumer laws), but online harm remains large - at least EUR 7.9 billion a year - and almost all popular websites still use manipulative designs.

indicators.objective: The 2003 UCPD proposal predates the legislative financial statement indicator sections; it set no monitoring indicators. The extended impact assessment framed success as more cross-border marketing and shopping and greater consumer confidence

indicators.indicator: More consumers buying cross-border and more firms marketing cross-border by replacing fragmented national fairness rules
indicators.target_or_baseline: Baseline: 13% of consumers made a cross-border purchase in the previous 12 months (Eurobarometer 2002)
indicators.evidence: One causal study (difference-in-differences on Eurobarometer data 2006-2014) links UCPD transposition to higher consumer trust and more cross-border purchases, but only in countries that had low protection before. Descriptively, 19.1% of EU individuals bought online from sellers in other EU countries in the last 3 months of 2023 (vs 48.2% from national sellers; Eurostat isoc_ec_ibos) - not comparable with the 2002 baseline and not attributable to the UCPD alone. Commission 2013 report: 52% of consumers interested in cross-border purchases (+19 points vs 2006).
indicators.sources: SEC(2003) 724; Rösner, Haucap & Heimeshoff 2020; COM(2013) 139; Eurostat isoc_ec_ibos

indicators.indicator: Fewer unfair (misleading/aggressive) practices and lower consumer detriment
indicators.evidence: Detriment remains high: the 2024 Digital Fairness Fitness Check conservatively estimates EUR 7.9bn a year of consumer detriment from problems online (UCPD, CRD and UCTD together). 97% of popular websites/apps used at least one dark pattern (2022 behavioural study); a 2023 CPC sweep found dark patterns in 148 of 399 online shops. Earlier sweeps: about 80% of websites found in breach were corrected after enforcement (2013 report).
indicators.sources: SWD(2024) 230/231; Lupiáñez-Villanueva et al. 2022; CPC sweep 2023; COM(2013) 139

indicators.indicator: Simpler regulatory environment, lower compliance costs for cross-border traders
indicators.evidence: 2017 Fitness Check judged compliance costs very proportionate, including for SMEs. 2024 Fitness Check estimates adjustment and administrative costs of the three core consumer directives at about EUR 511-737m a year EU-wide; only 10-18% of traders report high costs.

indicators.indicator: Effective and consistent enforcement across Member States
indicators.evidence: Recurring weak point: the 2024 Fitness Check rates effectiveness 'limited' citing insufficient public and private enforcement; Omnibus Directive (2019/2161) added fines of at least 4% of turnover for coordinated cross-border cases, but its 2024 implementation report says application is at an early stage.

literature.citation: European Commission (2003), Extended impact assessment on the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, SEC(2003) 724
literature.title: Extended impact assessment on the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive
literature.method: ex-ante (Eurobarometer surveys of 2,899 businesses and 16,129 consumers; consultation)
literature.outcomes: cross-border trade; consumer confidence; compliance costs
literature.headline: Divergent national fairness rules are a significant internal-market barrier; only 13% of consumers had bought cross-border in the past 12 months; harmonisation expected to raise cross-border marketing and purchases (not quantified)
literature.summary_plain: The Commission argued that one EU-wide set of rules on unfair selling would help firms sell, and consumers shop, across borders; it did not put a number on the gain.

literature.citation: European Commission (2013), First Report on the application of the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, COM(2013) 139
literature.title: First Report on the application of the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive
literature.headline: Directive judged to have removed obstacles and simplified rules; 52% of consumers interested in cross-border purchases (+19 points vs 2006); ~80% of websites found in breach in EU sweeps were corrected; enforcement, especially cross-border, needs strengthening; no amendment proposed
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's first review found the directive worked but said enforcement, especially across borders, had to improve.

literature.citation: European Commission (2017), Report of the Fitness Check of EU consumer and marketing law (incl. the UCPD), SWD(2017) 209
literature.title: Report of the Fitness Check of EU consumer and marketing law (incl. the UCPD)
literature.method: review (Civic Consulting support study, surveys, consultation)
literature.headline: Rules still largely fit for purpose if effectively enforced; compliance costs very proportionate, including for SMEs, so limited scope for burden reduction; led to the 2018 New Deal / Omnibus proposal on enforcement and modernisation
literature.summary_plain: The 2017 review concluded EU consumer rules were largely fit for purpose and cheap to comply with, but poorly known and unevenly enforced.

literature.citation: Rösner, Haucap & Heimeshoff (2020), The impact of consumer protection in the digital age: Evidence from the European Union, International Journal of Industrial Organization 73 (CESifo WP 8081)
literature.title: The impact of consumer protection in the digital age: Evidence from the European Union
literature.venue: International Journal of Industrial Organization 73 (CESifo WP 8081)
literature.method: causal: difference-in-differences with multiple periods (staggered UCPD transposition 2007-2010; Eurobarometer 2006-2014)
literature.headline: UCPD introduction significantly associated with higher consumer trust and more cross-border purchases, but only for countries with low consumer protection before the directive; effect grows over time then stabilises
literature.summary_plain: Countries that had weak consumer protection before the UCPD saw consumer trust and cross-border shopping rise after adopting it; countries that already had strong rules saw no clear change.

literature.citation: Lupiáñez-Villanueva, Boluda, Bogliacino et al. (for European Commission, DG JUST) (2022), Behavioural study on unfair commercial practices in the digital environment: dark patterns and manipulative personalisation, Publications Office of the EU, doi:10.2838/859030
literature.authors: Lupiáñez-Villanueva, Boluda, Bogliacino et al. (for European Commission, DG JUST)
literature.title: Behavioural study on unfair commercial practices in the digital environment: dark patterns and manipulative personalisation
literature.venue: Publications Office of the EU, doi:10.2838/859030
literature.method: mystery shopping of popular websites/apps; online experiments
literature.outcomes: prevalence of dark patterns; consumer behaviour
literature.headline: 97% of the most popular websites and apps used by EU consumers deployed at least one dark pattern; consumers have limited ability to recognise them
literature.summary_plain: Almost all of the most popular websites and apps used at least one manipulative design trick, years after the UCPD banned misleading and aggressive practices.

literature.citation: European Commission and CPC Network (2023), Sweep of online shops for dark patterns (press release IP/23/418), IP/23/418, 30 January 2023
literature.title: Sweep of online shops for dark patterns (press release IP/23/418)
literature.method: enforcement sweep (399 online shops, 23 Member States + NO, IS)
literature.headline: 148 of 399 online shops used at least one dark pattern (fake countdown timers, steering design, hidden information); 27 of 102 apps checked also did
literature.summary_plain: Consumer authorities found manipulative designs in almost 40% of online shops checked in 2022-23.

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Fitness Check of EU consumer law on digital fairness (executive summary SWD(2024) 231), SWD(2024) 230
literature.title: Fitness Check of EU consumer law on digital fairness (executive summary SWD(2024) 231)
literature.headline: Effectiveness 'limited': consumer detriment from online problems conservatively EUR 7.9bn a year; compliance costs of UCPD, CRD and UCTD about EUR 511-737m a year, only 10-18% of traders report high costs; enforcement insufficient; legal uncertainty on dark patterns, addictive design, influencer marketing, subscriptions
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's 2024 review found the UCPD and sister directives still relevant and cheap to comply with, but only partly effective online, with consumers losing at least EUR 7.9 billion a year.
literature.quality: self-evaluation; detriment estimate conservative and not attributable to the directives

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Report on the implementation of Directive (EU) 2019/2161 (Modernisation/Omnibus Directive), COM(2024) 258
literature.title: Report on the implementation of Directive (EU) 2019/2161 (Modernisation/Omnibus Directive)
literature.headline: Directive at an early stage of application; most Member States now provide fines of at least 4% of turnover for coordinated cross-border cases and individual remedies for victims of unfair practices; sweeps found 23% of price-reduction announcements breached the new rules
literature.summary_plain: The 2019 upgrade to the UCPD gave authorities bigger fines and consumers new remedies, but the Commission says it is too early to judge their effect.
